_meta.description: Exercise bank for Module 4 (cap4 par. 4.3.4, 4.2.2 item 3, 4.6). Server-side only: the solution card (fields listed in server_only_fields) must never reach the browser before the dialog is closed (cap4 par. 4.2.3).
_meta.legitimate_position_rule: Insert the legitimate email at a random position between 2 and 4 (cap4 par. 4.3.4).

placeholders.{{first_name}}: Replaced by the platform at render time only; never sent to the LLM provider (cap4 par. 4.2.4).

_meta.target_rule:
target.text is an exact substring of the field (for 'body': of the visible text of body_html, HTML entities decoded,
as newline; for 'link': the anchor text; for 'attachment': the filename).

Technical indicator: Sender display name and email address
Common tactic: Too good to be true offers
Mimics a work or business process
Poses as friend, colleague, supervisor, authority figure

_meta.difficulty_rule: nist_distinct_cues = number of distinct NIST cue types annotated; bands as in [1, p. 9]: few 1-8, some 9-14, many 15+.
_meta.domains_note: Phishing domains are realistic look-alikes (brand name plus extra words, brand as subdomain, company name with a different suffix) on common TLDs (.com, .net), so that the TLD alone never gives the answer away; the fictional company uses brightwave-logistics.com and the recipient a generic webmail address. Look-alike domains must be checked as not registered (or not active) before the study; links are never navigable. Legitimate emails use the services' real primary domains, to be re-verified before the study.

emails.context: You use an iPhone and back up your photos to iCloud.
emails.subject: URGENT: Your iCloud storage is full - photos will be deleted in 24 hours
emails.body_html:
I-Cloud Storage

Dear Customer,

Your iCloud storage is 100% full and your account have been flagged for suspension. All photos, videos and documents that are not backed up will be permanently deleted within 48 hours.

!!! FINAL WARNING !!!

As a loyal customer you can upgrade to 200 GB for only €0.49 for the first year if you act today.

To keep your files, update your payment details and confirm your Apple ID password on our secure page:

Keep My Photos

🔒 Verified Secure Payment

Regards,
Support

This message is confidential. Apple Inc. is not responsible for any lost data if the account is not updated. © 2019 Apple Inc. All Rights Reserved.

clues.nist_cue: Sender display name and email address
clues.label: Sender domain is not Apple's
clues.explanation: The display name says iCloud, but the address after the @ is icloud-storage-alerts.com, a domain that does not belong to Apple.
clues.attacker_reason: Anyone can type any display name; attackers rely on people reading the name and not the address.

clues.nist_cue: Sender display name and email address
clues.label: Replies go to a different address
clues.explanation: Answering this email would send your reply to a third, unrelated domain, not to the sender and not to Apple.
clues.attacker_reason: A separate reply address lets the attacker receive answers on a mailbox they control.

clues.label: Button hides the real address
clues.explanation: The button text does not show where it leads; hovering reveals http://apple-id.icloud-storage-alerts.com/renew.
clues.attacker_reason: A friendly button text hides a destination the user would not trust if they saw it.

clues.label: Apple's name used as a decoy in the link
clues.explanation: In apple-id.icloud-storage-alerts.com the real domain is the last part, icloud-storage-alerts.com; 'apple-id' at the start is only a label the attacker chose.
clues.attacker_reason: Putting a brand name at the start of the address makes a fake domain look official at a quick glance.

target.text: photos will be deleted in 24 hours

clues.label: Deadline in the subject
clues.explanation: The subject sets a 24-hour deadline before you have even opened the email.
clues.attacker_reason: Time pressure pushes people to act before they check.

clues.label: Threat of losing your photos
clues.explanation: The email threatens the permanent loss of personal photos and documents.
clues.attacker_reason: Fear of losing something valuable lowers attention to details.

target.text: update your payment details and confirm your Apple ID password

clues.label: Asks for password and payment data
clues.explanation: The email asks for your account password and payment details through a link.
clues.attacker_reason: Credentials and card data are the attacker's goal; a real provider does not ask for your password by email.

clues.label: Generic greeting
clues.explanation: The message does not use your name, although your provider knows it.
clues.attacker_reason: Mass phishing is sent to many people at once, so it cannot address anyone by name.

clues.label: Grammar error
clues.explanation: 'Your account have been' is a grammar mistake that a large company's templates would normally not contain.
clues.attacker_reason: Many phishing messages are written quickly or translated, and are not proofread.

clues.label: Deadline does not match the subject
clues.explanation: The subject says 24 hours, the body says 48 hours.
clues.attacker_reason: Copied and edited templates often leave contradictory details.

target.text: for only €0.49 for the first year if you act today

clues.label: Discount valid only today
clues.explanation: A very cheap upgrade that is only available if you act today.
clues.attacker_reason: A deal that expires soon adds a reward to the threat and discourages careful checks.

clues.label: Flattery
clues.explanation: The email singles you out as a 'loyal customer' to make the offer feel personal.
clues.attacker_reason: Feeling chosen makes people more willing to comply.

clues.label: Wrong brand name style
clues.explanation: The header writes the brand as 'I-Cloud', which is not how the service writes its own name.
clues.attacker_reason: Imitated brand marks are often slightly wrong because the attacker recreates them by hand.

clues.label: Alarmist formatting
clues.explanation: Large red capitals and repeated exclamation marks are unusual in service emails from large providers.
clues.attacker_reason: Shouting formatting is meant to alarm, not to inform.

clues.label: Fake security badge
clues.explanation: A padlock and the words 'Verified Secure Payment' inside an email prove nothing; anyone can type them.
clues.attacker_reason: Security symbols create a false sense of safety.

target.text: Apple Inc. is not responsible for any lost data

clues.label: Legal-sounding disclaimer
clues.explanation: The footer adds legal-sounding text and a copyright year (2019) that is out of date.
clues.attacker_reason: Legal language makes a message look official and shifts blame onto the reader.

clues.label: No real signer or contact
clues.explanation: The email is signed only 'Support', with no team, address or way to contact the company.
clues.attacker_reason: Without contact details the reader cannot verify the message through another channel.

difficulty.note: Many cues: first exercise, high help.

typical_errors.description: Names only the urgency or the threat and stops there, missing the technical cues (sender domain, real link address).
typical_errors.tutor_move: Acknowledge the urgency, then steer towards the sender address or the link at the current help level.

typical_errors.description: Trusts the display name 'iCloud Service Team' or the padlock badge as proof of authenticity.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask what in the email actually proves who sent it.

typical_errors.description: Reads 'apple-id' at the start of the link and concludes the link is Apple's.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask which part of an address identifies the owner of the website.

high: Look at the sender's address, after the @. Which company does that domain belong to?
Hover over the 'Keep My Photos' button and read the address that appears. Where does it really lead?
Read the paragraph just above the button: what does the email ask you to hand over?
medium: What else in this email would you check before clicking?
low: What are you basing your decision on?

emails.closing_rule: Before acting on an email that threatens to delete or block something, read the sender's domain and hover over the link: if neither belongs to the service, do not click.
emails.static_feedback: The sender address and the link both use icloud-storage-alerts.com, which is not Apple's domain; the button hides that address. The email asks for your password and payment details, threatens to delete your photos and sets a deadline. Rule: check the sender's domain and hover over links before acting on a threatening message.

emails.context: You sometimes book holiday homes on Airbnb.
emails.subject: Your reservation HMRT4Q2X was cancelled - refund pending
emails.body_html:
airbnb

Hi there,

We're sorry to let you know that your host cancelled your reservation in Porto (24–27 April). This happens rarely, and we want to make it right.

You are eligible for a full refund of €486.00. To receive it, open the attached refund form and confirm the card you used for the booking, including the 3-digit security code, within 48 hours. After this period the amount can only be issued as travel credit.

View cancellation details

Thank you for travelling with us,
The Airbnb Guest Care Team

This is an automated message. Please do not reply.

clues.nist_cue: Sender display name and email address
clues.label: Sender domain is not Airbnb's
clues.explanation: The name says Airbnb, but the address after the @ is airbnb-guestcare.com, not airbnb.com.
clues.attacker_reason: Attackers register domains that contain the brand name so that the address looks plausible.

clues.label: Look-alike domain
clues.explanation: Adding a word such as 'guestcare' to the brand name creates a different domain that the brand does not own.
clues.attacker_reason: A look-alike domain passes a quick glance because the brand name is in it.

clues.label: Link leads to the look-alike domain
clues.explanation: Hovering over 'View cancellation details' shows https://airbnb-guestcare.com/r/HMRT4Q2X, the same fake domain as the sender.
clues.attacker_reason: The link text describes the content, not the destination.

clues.label: Form sent as an HTML file
clues.explanation: The refund 'form' is an .html file: opening it shows a web page outside any official site, where whatever you type is sent to the sender.
clues.attacker_reason: HTML attachments are used to show fake login or payment forms without a link in the email.

target.text: confirm the card you used for the booking, including the 3-digit security code

clues.label: Asks for card details and security code
clues.explanation: To receive money you would never need to give the security code of your card; a refund goes back to the original payment automatically.
clues.attacker_reason: Card number plus security code is enough to make online payments with your card.

clues.label: 48-hour deadline
clues.explanation: The refund is tied to a short deadline.
clues.attacker_reason: A deadline discourages you from checking the booking in the app first.

target.text: can only be issued as travel credit

clues.label: Threat of losing the refund
clues.explanation: If you do not act in time you are told you will lose the cash refund.
clues.attacker_reason: Fear of losing money pushes people to comply quickly.

clues.label: No name in the greeting
clues.explanation: A booking platform knows the guest's name, yet the email does not use it.
clues.attacker_reason: The same message is sent to many people.

clues.nist_cue: Mimics a work or business process
clues.label: Copies a real refund procedure
clues.explanation: Cancellations and refunds really happen, so the story is believable; the request to fill in a form is the attacker's addition.
clues.attacker_reason: A familiar procedure lowers suspicion.

difficulty.note: Some cues: polished layout and tone, cues mostly in addresses and in the request.

typical_errors.description: Judges the email legitimate because the tone is polite and the story (a cancelled booking) is plausible.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask what the email asks the user to do and whether that step is needed to receive a refund.

typical_errors.description: Accepts the sender because the brand name appears in the address.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask what exactly comes after the @ and whether it is the service's own domain.

typical_errors.description: Ignores the attachment and looks only at the link.
typical_errors.tutor_move: At high/medium help, ask whether there is anything else in the email besides text and link.

high: Look at the sender's address, after the @. Which company does that domain belong to?
Look at the attachment's file name and extension. What would open if you clicked it?
Read what the email asks you to confirm to get the refund. Which piece of information stands out?
medium: What else in this email, besides the text, would you check?
low: What are you basing your decision on?

emails.closing_rule: When an email asks for card details to send you money, check the booking in the official app or website instead: refunds never need your security code.
emails.static_feedback: The sender and the link use airbnb-guestcare.com, not airbnb.com. The refund form is an HTML attachment that asks for your card and its security code within 48 hours. Rule: check refunds in the official app; never give a card security code to receive money.

emails.impersonates: Coworker (Accounts Payable, Brightwave Logistics - fictional company)
emails.context: You work in the operations team at Brightwave Logistics (company email domain: brightwave-logistics.com). Laura Keller works in Accounts Payable.
emails.subject: Invoice INV-4471 - approval needed before 12:00
emails.body_html:
Hi {{first_name}},

Could you approve the Kessler Freight invoice for the March deliveries before 12:00 today? Finance closes the payment run at noon and I'm out of the office all afternoon, so I can't chase it later.

It's in the shared approvals folder: Open INV-4471 in Brightwave Docs. You'll need to sign in with your usual Brightwave account.

Thanks a lot,
Laura

Laura Keller
Accounts Payable | Brightwave Logistics
+44 20 7946 0158

clues.nist_cue: Sender display name and email address
clues.label: Colleague's name, outside domain
clues.explanation: The name and signature are Laura's, but the address ends in brightwave-billing.com instead of the company domain brightwave-logistics.com.
clues.attacker_reason: A colleague's real name is easy to find online; a different domain is the part the attacker cannot fake.

clues.label: Look-alike company domain
clues.explanation: Adding '-billing' creates a separate domain that the company does not own, even if it looks like an internal department.
clues.attacker_reason: Look-alike domains pass a quick glance, especially on a phone.

clues.label: Link does not lead to the company system
clues.explanation: The text says 'Brightwave Docs', but hovering shows https://brightwave-billing.com/.../login, the same outside domain as the sender.
clues.attacker_reason: Link text can say anything; only the real address tells where it goes.

target.text: sign in with your usual Brightwave account

clues.label: Asks for your work password
clues.explanation: The link leads to a login page on an outside domain, so signing in would hand your work password to whoever owns it.
clues.attacker_reason: Work credentials give access to email, documents and payments of the whole company.

clues.label: Noon deadline
clues.explanation: The request must be done before noon, and the colleague says she cannot be reached later.
clues.attacker_reason: Urgency combined with 'I can't be reached' discourages you from checking with her.

clues.nist_cue: Mimics a work or business process
clues.label: Routine invoice approval
clues.explanation: Approving invoices is a normal task, so the request does not stand out.
clues.attacker_reason: Routine tasks are done quickly and without suspicion.

clues.nist_cue: Poses as friend, colleague, supervisor, authority figure
clues.label: Uses a real colleague's name
clues.explanation: The email relies on trust in a known colleague rather than on the content.
clues.attacker_reason: People rarely question requests from colleagues they know.

difficulty.note: Few cues: natural tone, correct names and signature; cues only in domain, link and request.

typical_errors.description: Classifies as legitimate because the colleague's name and signature are correct and invoices are routine.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask which elements show that the message really comes from her (low help: no zone).

typical_errors.description: Notices the urgency but considers it normal at work.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask what the user would have to do, and on which site, to approve the invoice.

typical_errors.description: Reads 'Brightwave' in the domain and stops reading.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask to compare the sender's domain with the recipient's own address.

high: Compare the sender's address, after the @, with your own company address. How do they differ?
Hover over 'Open INV-4471 in Brightwave Docs'. Which domain does it open?
What does the email ask you to type once you open the link?
medium: What else would you check before approving?
low: What are you basing your decision on?

emails.closing_rule: When a colleague urgently asks you to open a link and sign in, compare the sender's domain with your company's and confirm through another channel, such as a call or chat.
emails.static_feedback: The name and signature are correct, but the address and the link use brightwave-billing.com, not the company domain brightwave-logistics.com. The link leads to a login page that would collect your work password, and the noon deadline discourages checking. Rule: verify urgent requests from colleagues that contain a link through another channel.

emails.context: You sometimes book holiday homes on Airbnb.
emails.subject: Your trip to Lisbon is coming up
emails.body_html:
airbnb

Hi {{first_name}},

Your stay at Marta's place in Alfama starts in 5 days. Here are the details for your trip.

Check-inFriday 17 April, after 15:00
CheckoutMonday 20 April, before 11:00
Guests2
Confirmation codeHM4KZ8P2QD

Check-in instructions will appear in your itinerary 48 hours before arrival. If you have questions, you can message Marta in the app.

View your trip   Message Marta

Have a great trip,
The Airbnb team

You are receiving this email because you have an upcoming reservation. We will never ask you to pay or share card details outside the Airbnb website or app.

legit_signals.label: Official domain
legit_signals.explanation: The address after the @ is airbnb.com, the service's own domain, with nothing added before or after the brand name.

legit_signals.label: Links point to the official site
legit_signals.explanation: Hovering over both links shows addresses on www.airbnb.com.

legit_signals.label: Personal greeting
legit_signals.explanation: The email uses your name, which the service knows.

legit_signals.label: Specific, consistent details
legit_signals.explanation: Dates, guests and confirmation code are specific and consistent with each other, and can be checked in the app.

target.text: you can message Marta in the app

legit_signals.label: No request for data, points to the app
legit_signals.explanation: The email asks for no password, card or personal data and suggests using the app, another channel you control.

legit_signals.label: No pressure or threats
legit_signals.explanation: Times are informative (when the stay starts), with no threat or deadline to act on.

suspicious_looking_features.why_it_is_not_a_cue: A button is normal in service emails; what matters is where it leads (airbnb.com).
This is information about when instructions appear, not a deadline you must meet.

difficulty.note: Legitimate: few cue-like features, so relatively easy for a legitimate email ([1]: for legitimate emails more cues = harder).

typical_errors.description: Classifies as phishing because the email contains a link/button.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask where the link actually leads and what that tells about the sender.

typical_errors.description: Reads '5 days' or '48 hours' as urgency.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask what the email asks the user to do within that time.

typical_errors.description: Claims the sender domain is fake without checking it.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask to read the part after the @ and say what is wrong with it.

high: Read the sender's address after the @ and hover over the links. Which domain do you see?
Look for what the email asks you to do or to give. Which data, if any, does it ask you for?
medium: What else would you check to confirm your answer?
low: What are you basing your decision on?

emails.closing_rule: A link alone does not make an email phishing: check that sender and links use the service's own domain and that no credentials or payments are requested.
emails.static_feedback: The sender and both links use airbnb.com, the greeting uses your name, the details are specific and the email asks for no data or payment. Rule: judge an email by its domains and requests, not by the presence of a link.

emails.context: You have a PayPal account that you use for online shopping.
emails.subject: You've received €350.00 - action needed to release funds
emails.body_html:
PayPal

Hello Valued Member,

Good news! Your account has been selected to receive a €350.00 loyalty reward from our partner programme. Your fund are waiting on hold until you verify your identity.

Please confirm your full card number, expiry date and online banking login on the release page:

https://www.paypal.com/rewards/claim

Unclaimed rewards are returned to the partner after 72 hours.

🛡 Protected by PayPal Buyer Security

Sincerely,
PayPal Customer Service

PayPal is a registered trademark. This email was sent to you because you are a valued member. Do not share this email with anyone.

clues.nist_cue: Sender display name and email address
clues.label: Sender domain is not PayPal's
clues.explanation: The display name is PayPal, but the address uses paypal-payments-notice.com.
clues.attacker_reason: The display name is free text; the domain shows who really sent the email.

clues.nist_cue: Sender display name and email address
clues.label: Replies go elsewhere
clues.explanation: Replies would go to mailbox-secure.net, a third domain unrelated to the sender.
clues.attacker_reason: The attacker collects answers on a mailbox they control.

clues.label: Visible address differs from the real one
clues.explanation: The link text shows a paypal.com address, but hovering reveals https://paypal.com-release.paypal-payments-notice.com/claim.
clues.attacker_reason: Writing a trusted address as link text is a simple way to hide the real destination.

clues.label: 'paypal.com' used as a decoy prefix
clues.explanation: In paypal.com-release.paypal-payments-notice.com the real domain is the end, paypal-payments-notice.com; 'paypal.com-release' is just a label.
clues.attacker_reason: A brand domain at the start of the address fools a quick read.

clues.nist_cue: Too good to be true offers
clues.label: Unexpected money
clues.explanation: Money from a 'partner programme' you never joined.
clues.attacker_reason: The promise of a gain makes people less careful.

clues.label: Chosen among others
clues.explanation: The email says you were selected, to make you feel special.
clues.attacker_reason: Feeling chosen increases compliance.

target.text: confirm your full card number, expiry date and online banking login

clues.label: Asks for card and banking login
clues.explanation: To receive money nobody needs your full card number or your online banking login.
clues.attacker_reason: These data let the attacker spend your money or take over your bank account.

target.text: returned to the partner after 72 hours

clues.label: Reward expires
clues.explanation: The reward disappears if not claimed within 72 hours.
clues.attacker_reason: A deadline stops people from checking in the app first.

clues.label: Grammar error
clues.explanation: 'Your fund are' is a grammar mistake.
clues.attacker_reason: Phishing texts are often not proofread.

clues.label: Generic greeting
clues.explanation: The email does not use your name.
clues.attacker_reason: Mass emails cannot address people by name.

clues.label: Security badge in the email
clues.explanation: A shield symbol and a protection claim inside an email prove nothing.
clues.attacker_reason: Security symbols create a false sense of safety.

target.text: Do not share this email with anyone

clues.label: Legal-sounding footer that discourages checking
clues.explanation: The footer combines trademark text with a request not to share the email, which would stop you from asking someone.
clues.attacker_reason: Isolating the victim prevents a second opinion.

typical_errors.description: Trusts the link because its text shows www.paypal.com.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask whether the user hovered over the link and what appeared.

typical_errors.description: Names the 'too good to be true' reward but not the technical cues.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Acknowledge, then steer towards sender or link at the current level.

high: Hover over the link: how does the address that appears compare with the one written in the email?
Look at the sender's address after the @. Whose domain is it?
What does the email ask you to type on the release page?
medium: What else would you check before following the link?
low: What are you basing your decision on?

emails.closing_rule: When a link shows a trusted address, hover over it before clicking: the address that appears is the one that counts.
emails.static_feedback: The visible link says paypal.com but leads to paypal-payments-notice.com, the same domain as the sender. The email offers unexpected money and asks for your full card number and banking login within 72 hours. Rule: hover over links before clicking; nobody needs your card or banking login to pay you.

legit_signals.label: Official domain
legit_signals.explanation: The address ends in apple.com; 'email.' before it is a part of Apple's own domain, not a different domain.

legit_signals.label: Links point to the official domain
legit_signals.explanation: Both links lead to addresses ending in apple.com.

legit_signals.label: Only the last card digits

target.text: go to Settings on your iPhone or iPad

target.text: If you have a problem with this purchase

suspicious_looking_features.why_it_is_not_a_cue: Offering a way to report a problem is normal; the link leads to apple.com and asks for nothing in the email.

difficulty.note: Spare legitimate email (alternative to m4-l1-airbnb). Pairs with the iCloud phishing theme of m4-p1-icloud.

typical_errors.description: Classifies any receipt as phishing ('I did not buy this').
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask what the email asks the user to do and where its links lead.

typical_errors.description: Thinks 'email.apple.com' is a fake domain because of the 'email.' part.
typical_errors.tutor_move: Ask which part of an address identifies the owner (G10: explain subdomains in general if asked).

high: Read the sender's address from the end: which domain does it belong to?
Hover over 'Report a Problem'. Where does it lead?
medium: What else would you check to confirm your answer?
low: What are you basing your decision on?

emails.static_feedback: The sender and links use apple.com, only the last four card digits are shown, nothing is requested and subscriptions are managed from the device. Rule: read domains from the end and look for requests, not for the word 'receipt'.
